description: Temporary files that apps keep to load faster next time. Apps rebuild them automatically, so removing them only costs a slightly slower first launch.
Safari's web cache and favicons. Removing it is safe but pages load slower the first time and some sites may ask you to sign in again.
Spotify's offline song cache. Removing it frees space but downloaded tracks must be fetched again and you may need to sign in.
Slack's message and image cache. Removing it is safe but Slack reloads your workspaces and may sign you out.
Microsoft Teams cache. Removing it is safe but Teams will rebuild it and usually asks you to sign in again.
iCloud Drive's sync cache. Removing it can stall uploads and re-download every iCloud file, so it is never offered for cleanup.
CloudKit and iCloud Photos sync state. Removing it forces a full re-sync and can lose pending changes, so it is never offered for cleanup.
In-progress background downloads managed by macOS. Removing it breaks transfers that apps are waiting on, so it is never offered for cleanup.
Apple ID, Spotlight and HomeKit working data. Removing it can sign you out of iCloud or break search, so it is never offered for cleanup.
Diagnostic logs written by apps and system services. They are only useful for troubleshooting and apps start new ones automatically.
Log files kept by sandboxed apps. They are only useful for troubleshooting and the app writes new ones as it runs.
Crash and hang reports collected when an app misbehaved. They help developers debug but have no effect on your apps if removed.
Xcode build products and indexes. Xcode regenerates them on the next build, so removing them only makes the next build slower.
Contains dSYMs for shipped builds. Without them you cannot symbolicate crash reports from released apps, so keep archives you may still need.
Debug symbols copied from devices you plugged in. Xcode copies them again the next time that device is connected.
Simulator runtime caches. The simulator rebuilds them on next launch, so removing them is safe.
Xcode's download and documentation cache. Xcode re-downloads whatever it needs, so removing it is safe.
Items you already moved to the Trash. Emptying it deletes them permanently and frees their space.
Partial downloads that were interrupted and never finished. They cannot be opened; start the download again if you still need the file.
Installer images and archives downloaded more than a month ago. The app is usually already installed; keep any archive you have not unpacked yet.
Downloaded Ollama models, re-download to restore. Each model can be several gigabytes and must be pulled again before Ollama can use it.
Hugging Face model and dataset cache. Libraries download these again on demand, which can take a long time for large models.
LM Studio models and cache. Removing them deletes every downloaded model; you must download them again inside LM Studio.
PyTorch pretrained weights cache. PyTorch downloads the weights again when a script asks for them.
pip's download cache for Python packages. pip fetches packages again on the next install, so removing it is safe.
Homebrew's downloaded bottles and casks. Homebrew re-downloads anything it needs, so removing them is safe.
npm's package tarball cache. npm fetches packages again on the next install.
Yarn's package cache. Yarn fetches packages again on the next install.
Gradle's dependency and build cache. Gradle downloads dependencies again on the next build, which can take a while on slow connections.
Maven's local repository of downloaded dependencies. Maven re-downloads them on the next build, which can take a while for large projects.
Cargo's cache of downloaded Rust crates. Cargo fetches crates again on the next build.
CocoaPods spec and pod cache. CocoaPods downloads pods again on the next install.
Swift Package Manager's repository cache. SwiftPM clones packages again on the next resolve.
pip's download cache for Python packages. pip fetches packages again on the next install, so removing it is safe.
Docker Desktop's virtual disk holding every image, container and volume. Removing it deletes all local Docker data; use 'docker system prune' to reclaim space safely instead.
Purgeable space macOS can reclaim: local Time Machine snapshots and files already in iCloud. macOS frees it automatically when needed; this reclaims it now.
